newsitem.title: INDIA: India says coffee futures mart must help growers.
newsitem.headline: India says coffee futures mart must help growers.

text.p: The Indian government would back a domestic coffee futures exchange as long as it safeguarded the interests of growers and consumers, a senior government official said on Monday.
"If you come up with a proper structure, I am sure it will receive support of the government," Deepak Chatterji, a senior official of Commerce Ministry said.
"The Coffee Board will encourage such a step," Chatterji told a workshop on a domestic coffee futures contract organised at the government-run Coffee Board's initiative.
He did not envisage a role for the Board in such an exchange.
"The Coffee Board's role will be confined to development, research and promoting coffee production, trading will be left to others," he said.

Chatterji said India aimed to produce 300,000 tonnes of coffee by the end of 2002. The Coffee Board estimates 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) coffee production at 205,000 tonnes, down from the previous estimates of 215,000 tonnes.

India exported 164,403 tonnes of coffee worth $410.75 million in 1996/97 (April-March) compared with 170,990 tonnes in 1995/96 valued at $456.00 million, Commerce Minister B.B. Ramaiah said on Friday.
Ramaiah told parliament India had set a coffee export target of 150,000 tonnes for 1997/98.
Chatterji said adequate safeguards were needed to prevent speculators from entering the market. "Any market system is welcome which takes care of consumers, growers and traders."
K.N. Kabra, who headed a government-committee on futures trading, said a start should be made only after framing policy objectives and getting the required expertise.
Kabra said the exchange should ensure the interests of growers and domestic consumers were taken account of as well as traders and exporters.
"Small growers, who constitute a majority of producers, should form cooperatives to trade on the exchange," Kabra said. "This is very important for the success of the exchange."
Coffee Board chairman Philipose Mathai said a coffee futures exchange would provide a transparent free market environment where members could trade futures and options.
